newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan trade surplus jumps amid renewed trade fears.
newsitem.headline: Japan trade surplus jumps amid renewed trade fears.

text.p: Japan's trade surplus rose sharply in June according to figures released on Friday -- news which is expected to fan recently re-ignited trade frictions with the United States.
Japan said the surplus in its current account -- the broadest measure of trade in goods and services -- rose 55.8 percent in June from a year earlier to 1.02 trillion yen.
The surplus in merchandise trade alone rose 18.7 percent in June from the same month a year earlier to 1.1 trillion yen.
At Friday's rate of around 119 yen to the dollar, the current account surplus in June stood at $8.5 billion and the merchandise trade surplus was $9.2 billion.
In the first six months of the calendar year, the current account surplus rose 40.4 percent.
A rise had been widely anticipated as Japan's customs-cleared trade surplus for June, which was announced last month, showed a 27.7 percent rise.
The trade surplus within the current account category, calculated on different basis, differs slightly from the customs-cleared trade surplus.

Japanese officials appeared to try to play down the news, saying they saw no sign of continuing large rises. Officials also said a rise in the national sales tax on April 1 had contributed to the surplus since it slowed down domestic demand for all goods.

But the figures were at the top end of analysts' expectations and did not bode well for the Japanese government, which is facing U.S. charges that Japan is trying to export its way out of its long-running economic slump.

"We think it's inevitable that trade friction will increase. The main reason for this is Japanese manufacturers are facing very weak demand at home so they've been forced to look to overseas markets to sell their goods," Richard Jerram, chief economist at ING Barings Securities in Tokyo, told Reuters Financial Television.

Earlier this week, U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky said U.S. officials were concerned that car exports to Japan had decreased and the trade deficit with Japan in general was deteriorating.

The markets took the news calmly with the dollar little changed against the Japanese yen. Tokyo stocks showed little interest, with attention focused instead on the flotation of a television group. After 30 minutes of trading, the Nikkei 225-share average was off a modest 0.43 percent at 19,391.34.
